frontmatter_description: Judge whether an utterance is adapted to fit the listener's knowledge, age, identity, or stance, rather than aimed at persuading, deceiving, or being polite.
title: Audience Calibration
use_when: Use when the task is to judge or choose wording that fits a particular listener's expertise, age, group membership, or prior stance.
Use when the decisive variable is whether the speaker adjusted explanation depth, vocabulary, examples, or framing for that audience.
Use when two phrasings carry the SAME goal and the question is only which one the listener can best understand or accept.
Use when the issue is listener-fit, not influence, truth, or politeness.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the goal is to change the listener's belief, attitude, or behavior; that is the persuasion-strategy capability (micro-41).

Do not use when the question is whether the statement is misleading, true, false, or selectively framed; that is the truth-status capability (micro-37) or the misleading-expression capability (micro-38).
Do not use when the question is WHY the speaker chose that wording (politeness, face-saving, testing); that is the speaker-motivation capability (micro-39).
Do not use when the issue is tact, embarrassment, faux pas, or offense; that is the faux-pas-and-offense capability (micro-42).
decision_variable: how well the expression fits the listener's knowledge, age, identity, or stance
trigger_checklist: Who is the target listener — expert, novice, child, insider, outsider, ally, or opponent?
Does the wording match that listener's likely background knowledge and vocabulary?
Do the candidate options share the same goal and differ only in how understandable or acceptable they are to this listener?
Would a different audience need a different level of detail, example, or tone for the SAME message?
workflow: Identify the target listener and what they likely know, value, or can follow.
Confirm the question is about listener-fit, not about changing the listener's mind, the truth of the claim, or the speaker's motive.
Compare the options on a single axis: which one is pitched at the right level of detail, vocabulary, and framing for this listener.
Reject options that add jargon a novice cannot follow, talk down to or dismiss the listener, or switch the task to persuasion.
Pick the option whose form best matches the audience profile; if the real task is to change the listener, exit to the persuasion-strategy capability.

special_case.title: Same content, two audiences
special_case.rule: When the same information is delivered to two listeners, the better-calibrated version is the one matched to the named listener's level — lower jargon for a novice, more technical depth for an expert. Do not average across listeners; calibrate to the one the question targets.

worked_example.scene: A doctor explains the same treatment twice: to a medical intern using clinical terms (BID dosing, adverse-event monitoring), and to the patient's parent who has no medical training, using everyday words ('a medicine taken twice a day, and here are the side effects in plain language').
worked_example.question: Which explanation is better calibrated to the patient's parent?
worked_example.answer_logic: The decision variable is listener-fit. For the lay parent the plain-language version is better calibrated because it removes jargon and matches their background knowledge; the clinical version fits the intern, not the parent.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to the persuasion-strategy capability — how to change the listener's belief, attitude, or behavior (micro-41) — if the core goal is to move the listener, not just to fit their level.
Exit to the misleading-expression capability — whether a true statement induces a false belief (micro-38) — if the issue is hidden implication, not audience fit.
Exit to the speaker-motivation capability — why the speaker chose that wording (micro-39) — if the question asks for the speaker's social motive.
Exit to the faux-pas-and-offense capability (micro-42) — tact, offense, and faux pas — if the central issue is embarrassment or rudeness rather than comprehension fit.

references.route_signal: Use this capability when the scene asks whether speech is adapted to a listener's expertise, age, identity, or stance, and the options differ mainly in how understandable or acceptable they are to that listener.
hard_boundary: Not about changing the listener's belief or behavior (that is the persuasion-strategy capability, micro-41).
Not about whether the message is true, false, or misleading (that is the truth-status or misleading-expression capability, micro-37/38).
Not about why the speaker chose the wording (that is the speaker-motivation capability, micro-39).
Not about whether the listener is offended or embarrassed (that is the faux-pas-and-offense capability, micro-42).
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not treat every tailored message as persuasion; matching a listener's level can be neutral and informative.
Do not pick the option that aims to change the listener's decision when the question only asks which wording fits them.
Do not infer the speaker's motive from audience-fit alone.
Do not collapse audience calibration into social tact or group politeness.
common_failure_modes: Confusing audience fit with persuasion strategy and choosing the most convincing option rather than the most understandable one.
Confusing audience fit with implied meaning or hidden implication.
Answering from the speaker's motive instead of the listener's needs.
Overweighting tone or warmth while ignoring whether the listener's knowledge level is matched.

minimal_pair.case: A clinician explains a diagnosis to a colleague in clinical terms and to a lay parent in plain everyday words; the question is which version fits the lay parent.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Both versions carry the same content; the only decisive variable is which is pitched at the listener's level of understanding.

minimal_pair.case: Xiao Hong wants to study computer science in another city; her parents prefer local medicine; the question is which appeal best brings her parents around.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Near miss: the wording is chosen to change the parents' decision, not just to fit their knowledge. Route to the persuasion-strategy capability (micro-41).

boundary_stress_test: A speaker simplifies a message to make the listener AGREE more easily: if influence is the goal, route to the persuasion-strategy capability (micro-41).
A speaker phrases something vaguely to hide a criticism: if hidden meaning or false inference is the issue, this is not audience calibration.
A speaker changes wording to avoid insulting an out-group: if tact or offense is central, route to the faux-pas-and-offense capability (micro-42).
A speaker asks WHY a careful phrasing was chosen: if the answer is a social motive, route to the speaker-motivation capability (micro-39).
references.generalization_note: Generalize by checking listener-fit across knowledge, age, identity, and stance: the same message re-pitched for a different audience. The decisive variable is comprehension and acceptability fit, not influence, truth, or motive. This applies across benchmark and real-world settings, with no dependence on any fixed item format.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: The same content is delivered to a named listener and the correct answer is the version pitched at that listener's level (low jargon for a novice, technical depth for an expert).
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The wording is chosen to change the listener's decision (persuasion), not merely to fit their level.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: An appeal is tailored to what the listener values, but the goal is still to change their decision, so it routes to persuasion.

notes: Keep the answer anchored in audience fit, not speaker intent or influence.
The decisive question is whether the expression is appropriately pitched for the named listener.
The nearest confusable cases are persuasion items; positives are best illustrated with clean made-up calibration scenes (e.g. explaining to an expert versus a novice).
core_question: Adapt expression to experts, novices, children, out-groups, or other listeners
